seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 6: Whose Seconds Are These
blurb: Petra accuses the wrong teammate before a match against the Guild's own side, and the truth arrives too late to save the night.

blocks.text: Drewe came back at a run. I saw her hands before I saw her face: the left one closing on the far sleeve of Lisle's coat, the right one still gripping her screwdriver against the cloth, both of them white across the knuckles.
'Pull when I pull,' she said.

We pulled. Lisle came over backwards between us as stiff as a wardrobe and as heavy as one, her lifted hand still at her hair. Her boot heels scraped the setts. We got her over the near rail, and then the far one. The tram bell rang at the corner and kept ringing.

I watched Drewe's hands. They did not let go and they did not change their grip. We made the kerb with Lisle's heels still in the gutter, and the tram went by behind us close enough that I felt the air of it on the back of my neck.
Drewe let go. Her hands were shaking so hard that the screwdriver fell out of the right one and rang in the gutter.

We propped Lisle against the post of the stop. Her eyes were still on the tram window where I had been sitting. A man at the back of the queue looked at us, and then at the clock, and then at his watch.
I picked up the screwdriver and held it out. Drewe took it in both hands, as if holding it would stop them. It did not.
'I saw your tram at the bend,' she said. 'I thought you had her.'

Lisle came out of it four minutes later by my watch. Her hand finished pushing the hair off her forehead. Her foot came down on the kerb instead of the rail, and she sat down hard on the step of the stop and looked at the tram lines, and at us, and at the tram going away down the hill.
She said nothing. She did not bet on anything. Drewe sat down beside her, put the screwdriver in her pocket and kept her hand in there with it.
I rode with Lisle to the warehouse. She told her foreman, and he wrote the stall in his book and gave her the broom.
That night at the desk I put my notebook beside the team sheets. I keep a copy of every sheet I lodge.
The variance column ran down the right-hand page. I wrote the roles out beside it.
MD7: Drewe Winder, Lisle the only Sprinter. Forty-seven over, warm.
MD8: no Winder, Lisle and Drewe both Sprinting. No variance. Cold.
MD9: Drewe Winder, Lisle the only Sprinter. Thirty-five over, warm.

The figures were right. I had weighed all three jars myself. By the printed rule, seconds wound in from catch-brass and left unspent go back to the jar at the end of the round, and if they are less than a day old they go back warm. Only a Winder can wind. Drewe was my only Winder both times. Seconds wound into a player are wound into her to be spent, and both times there was one player on the sheet whose work was spending them.
That much I could prove. The rest was my verdict, and I gave it to myself plainly.

Drewe's hands were hired. I had watched her pay her family's account on Spindle Row in clean new coins and say the shop had had a good week, when she had told me the week before that it took in two pocket watches and a carriage clock. The seconds, and the money, came through Lisle. She had carried illegal paper with Felix Wardle for two seasons and told nobody until the stalls made her. Someone who has dealt with a Reckoner who Defers knows where else seconds can be had. And a Sprinter knows what is in her hands. She spends out of them every round. If there were thirty seconds in her that I had not issued, she knew they were there, and she left them.
I knew what the Laws said a Reckoner should do with a breach. The Bank's spot-check clerk would take it at my next Close. Any Arbiter would take it on any landing. I knew the way to both.
I closed the notebook and locked it in the drawer.
On the sixth day Cassius sent for me at four, when I came in for the filing.

He had the quarter's winding returns for the stair towers stacked on his desk, untied. 'I shall want these reconciled and on this desk by half past twelve tomorrow night, Miss Sandor,' he said. 'The committee sits early the following morning, and I prefer to have read a thing before I am asked about it.'
Half past twelve the next night was the middle of my Close. He knew where I would be at midnight. He would be there himself, on the other side of the Arbor.
'Tomorrow night I'm on a stair-tower inspection,' I said.

'Then before it. I have every confidence in you.' He squared the stack with his fingertips and folded his hands on the blotter. 'Your father kept untidy logs too, Miss Sandor. I am sure you will want to be quite certain of these.'

I looked at his hands. They were folded right over left. The nails were cut short and square, and there was a Guild ring on the third finger of the right hand. The left thumb lay along the right one. They did not move. I watched them until I could trust my voice, and then I did not use it. I picked up the returns and went back to my desk.
So he had read the file. I had believed since March that the committee had. It was the first time anyone at the Guild had said so to my face.

The Bank's envelope was on my desk, under the pen the first clerk had left there. It was signed for the Office of Issue, and the signature could not be read. The Bank's own scale, it said, had been found to read thirty-five seconds high at the Ninth Stair Close. Calibration error. The result stands.

I wrote it into the variance column. The first ruling had said the porter's-lodge scale read forty-seven high. This one said the Bank's own scale read thirty-five high, and its zero had been checked before I weighed. Both rulings had fallen the same way, and both times the fault was in a scale.
The win stood. We had eleven points.

I did the winding returns at the desk that night and the next afternoon, and had them on his blotter at five past eleven on match night. There were two transposed figures in the south tower. I marked both.
The Regulars play on the landing the Copper Stair left empty. Lisle had played two seasons on it.

She was up there first, at the rail, with her hands in her coat pockets. I told her alone, before the others came up. I told her the three jars and the three sheets, the forty-seven and the thirty-five, warm both times, and that by the printed rule the seconds had gone into her and come back to the jar unspent. Then I told her my verdict: the seconds were hers, through Wardle's people, and Drewe was paid to wind them.
'I'm not taking it to the Bank,' I said. 'Or to an Arbiter. I won't report a teammate.'
I did not tell her why.
Lisle went very quiet. Her hands stayed in her pockets. She looked at me for a long time, and then at the ring.
'Two coppers says you're wrong,' she said.
That was all she said to me before the stroke.
Drewe came up the stair with Tran behind her and his chicory jug. I took Drewe to one side.
'Tonight you wind what I issue,' I said. 'Nothing else.'

She turned the screwdriver over in her fingers. 'Wind what's issued. Strictly by the train,' she said. 'I'll be the best-regulated thing on this landing.' She looked at the screwdriver while she said it, and then at the stair, and not at me.
My verdict was that she was ashamed of being hired. I did not ask her who had hired her. I thought I knew.

The Rate Board had IV and VIII at double and every other plate at true rate. We were away and defended VI. The Regulars fielded five: two Sprinters, Oakes and Pell, a Stiller on XI and their Keep on XII. We fielded four. Tran kept VI. Drewe wound. Lisle was our only Sprinter.
Cassius stood across the Arbor from me with his jar at his feet and wished me good evening by name. At the stroke the Arbiter put three hundred in my hands.
'Lisle, thirty.'
'Held.'
It was the only word she said all night. I issued her eleven times, and eleven times she said it, and nothing else. She did not bet. She did not look at the Arbor between rounds.

Their wall did not move. Every run Lisle made at XII she made past the Stiller on XI and into the Keep, and in five rounds she was Spilled five times. I gave Drewe nothing to wind. She stood where I put her, a frozen body for Lisle to run behind, and when the Lulls ended she was always exactly where she had been. Four against five is thinner than it looks on a sheet, and without a second spender we had no run to make.

So I played the bank. Cassius banked heavily or not at all, and never twice heavily in a row. I won seven bank points on forty-five seconds. The Regulars ran twice from the plates beside VI, in rounds five and seven, and scored both. Eight to seven, theirs.

In round nine the Token started on IX and Oakes ran it towards VI. Lisle spent twelve to meet him. When the Lull ended the Token lay dead on VII and Oakes was standing over it with his hand out. Tran told me, 'She caught him on seven. Mm. He never got to me.' I asked Lisle where she had touched him. She said, 'Held,' when I issued her the next round, and that was her answer.
After eleven rounds the Tally gave us two hundred and fourteen spent and forty-five banked. Forty-one in the jar. The Regulars' Tally left them thirty-eight.

Round twelve starts on XII, their own Hour plate: the furthest start on the ring from VI. Both their runs had come from the plates either side of VI. Every run they had started further out, Tran or Lisle had Spilled. If I issued Lisle and she spent to meet a run, my jar would fall below their thirty-eight and the bank point would be Cassius's. If I kept the forty-one, the bank point was mine whatever he wrote, and the bank point made it eight each. A draw.
There was another reason, and I gave it to myself plainly. I did not want seconds in Lisle's hands that night that I could not account for.
I issued no one.
Cassius watched me not issue. His Keep stepped off XII onto the dead floor, and Oakes stepped on and lifted the Token.
Then the Token was on VI, and the round was over.
I rebuilt it in the Bank minute from the Tally, from Tran and from the Arbiter, because I had seen none of it.
The Tally: Regulars, twenty more spent. Fourteen and six.

Tran's account. In live play, before Oakes lifted, their Stiller had walked off XI round the outside of the ring and stood on the dead floor at VI's rim, on the VII side. Pell stood on V. Oakes said 'Spend fourteen' as he lifted, and Tran's Set Still sprang. Tran watched him come round: XI, X, past Drewe frozen on IX, past Lisle frozen on VIII, onto VII. Then their Stiller was between Tran and VII, tall and frozen on the dead floor, and he lost sight of Oakes behind her. Pell said 'Spend six' on V and put his toe up to VI's edge on the V side.
'I turned to his feet,' Tran said. 'Mm. Millrace taught me that. First foot on your plate.' He rubbed his eyes. 'The other one came on behind me from seven and put it down.'
The Arbiter said, 'Clean. Two points, Regulars.'
Their jar was eighteen. Cassius wrote eighteen. I wrote nineteen. The bank point was ours, and it made the score eight to ten.
When the other results came in we were eleventh, on eleven points.

The Close was in the porter's lodge at the foot of the tower. The spot-check clerk checked the scale's zero in front of me, and I weighed the jar. Three hundred, less two hundred and fourteen spent: eighty-six. The dial said eighty-six. Cold in my hands.
'Eighty-six,' I said. 'No variance. Cold.'

I wrote all two hundred and fourteen of Lisle's seconds into her sleep: half an hour from three on six nights, and thirty-four minutes on the seventh. I read her each line. She said yes to every one, and nothing else.
At the next table Cassius weighed his own jar and declared it in a sentence. Then he came to my table and stood with his hands folded.
'Admirably thorough, Miss Sandor,' he said. 'And the returns were on my desk at five past eleven. I noticed.'
'Two figures transposed in the south tower,' I said. 'I've marked them.'
He inclined his head and went out.

We went back up to the landing because nobody wanted to go home. Tran sat on the bench with his jug. Lisle stood at the rail. Drewe stood in the middle of the ring on plate VI, where Tran had been, and turned the screwdriver over twice, and then put it in her pocket.
'Stop,' she said. 'All of you. I've a thing to say and I can't say it with a joke on.'
She took the brass snuffbox out of her coat and put it on the bench beside Tran.

'There's a man called Dunstan Mabry,' she said. 'Sponsors a Queue side. He calls it a little arrangement. He fills this the afternoon before every match. He puts a card in the lid with the times on, round letters like a copybook, and he takes the card back when he takes the box back. I wind it into whoever's Sprinting. In live play, between Lulls. A hand on the back when she runs past me, and the other hand on the box in my pocket.' She looked at Lisle. 'Into you. Every time I've been Winder.'
'For what?' I said.

'He said it was a sponsor's top-up. He said the League won't let a sponsor top up a side in the open, so it's done quiet. He pays me in new coins. The shop's account is nearly clear.' She stopped. 'It's full now. He filled it this afternoon. I never touched it tonight.'
I picked the box up in my bare hand. It was warm.
Lisle had not moved from the rail.
'I never count what's left,' she said. 'You say thirty, I say held, I spend what I need, the rest goes back. I've never once counted it. I wouldn't have known if there was a hundred in me.'
Nobody said anything.

'In nine,' Lisle said, 'when I went for Oakes. I saw Pell on five with his toe out, and their Stiller stood on the floor by seven, waiting for Tran to turn. I knew what it was. I didn't tell you.' She looked at me. 'You'd just told me I was a thief. I wasn't telling you anything.'
My figures had been right, all three jars. The person I had put to them was wrong.
'I was wrong, Marguerite,' I said. 'I said the seconds were yours and you were hiding them. They weren't yours, and you weren't hiding anything. It cost us the match.'
She looked at me for a moment when I said her name. Then she held out her hand, palm up.
I put two coppers in it.
Then I laid out the rest for all of them, and I did not tell them what to do with it.

I told them what was printed. Private possession of catch-brass is a lifetime ban from the Arbiters' Court and a prosecution by the Bank. Marguerite had never spent a wound-in second, so there were no Thefts. The friction on Drewe's transfers was charged to Drewe, and she had been paying it in stalls. Both jars had been declared honestly and both had been ruled calibration errors, and the results stood. Four is the fewest a side may field, so without Drewe we would forfeit every match left in the Turn.
I told them what was not printed. Whether the Bank could open a ruling it had already made, I did not know, and I would not guess.
'I'm not deciding this,' I said. 'We are.'
Tran opened his eyes. 'Keep her,' he said. 'Mm.'
'Keep her,' Marguerite said. 'She's on the first round every week till the Turn ends.'
Drewe opened her mouth and shut it again.
'Keep her, and say nothing outside this landing,' I said. 'Yes or no.'
Tran said yes. Marguerite said yes. Drewe said yes, very quietly. I said it last.
Drewe put the box back in her coat. Nobody told her to.
I went back to the Guild at twenty to two to lock up my key. The night desk was dark. The drawer was locked, as I had left it at half past eleven.
Two keys open that drawer. One was in my hand. The other belongs to the Guild.
On the bottom of the drawer, where my key lies on other nights, there was a card. The letters were round and friendly, like a copybook's, the way Drewe had said.
It said: 'Your promotion was never yours to have, Miss Sandor.'
